Group dynamics are the interpersonal relationships that develop between group members.�

The ways small groups form are significant. Social power which is held by the individual has the potential for causing change.� Social influence describes the formation and change of attitudes, opinions and behaviors through group interaction.� If group loyalty is fairly well established, the group will have a lot of influence on its members.

How can a group influence individual members? �People with an external locus of control feel that things outside of themselves control their fate.� People with internal locus of control feel their own resources and self-determination shape their destiny.� The person with the internal locus of control is less awed by authority figures and may react negatively to persuasion, while those with external locus of control will be more easily persuaded.

Social support is an important facto because when the group agrees, the individual has more confidence in the decision.� The acceptable group-defined behaviors are called social norms.�

The main idea of the risky-shift hypothesis is that a group will be more brave and daring in its actions and final decisions than a person acting alone.��For example, if students are unhappy about a rule at school, they are more likely to speak to administration about it as a group, than as an individual.

The opposite idea is the cautious-shift hypothesis.� The group may be more conservative than individual members.��For example a group of stranded campers may have a few people that want to try to find their way out of the bush, put the group decides to stay together and send up flares to help them be found.
